scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Bele originated from African fertility dances brought to the Caribbean by enslaved peoples and evolved through plantation-era social life.
It is considered possibly the oldest Creole dance in the French West Indies.
In Martinique, it developed among the 'Nouveaux Libres' (freed slaves) in rural areas called mornes between 1860 and 1960, symbolizing social values like mutual aid and resistance.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Bele is performed during social celebrations, full moon nights, funeral wakes (lavèyé), and work-related gatherings.
It embodies social values of solidarity, mutual aid, and cultural resistance.
The dance and music serve as a medium for community bonding, storytelling, and expressing life events such as fertility, mourning, and joy.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music centers on the bélé drum, a large tambour played with hands, accompanied by the tibwa—two wooden sticks striking a bamboo mounted on a stand—and the chacha (maracas).
The tibwa maintains a steady rhythmic pattern, while the drum marks accents and improvises.
Listen for the bélé drum (large tambour), tibwa (two wooden sticks on bamboo), chacha (maracas).

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: In Trinidad, female dancers wear plain underskirts with bright, flowing overskirts and matching headpieces, while male costumes are simpler with subtle references to female attire.
Performances occur during full moon evenings, funeral wakes, holidays, and festivals such as Easter and Independence Day.
The setting is communal, often outdoors or in social halls, with musicians, dancers, and audience forming an interactive circle or open space.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Variants exist across Caribbean islands: Dominica's bélé includes dances like bélé soté and bélé priòrité; Martinique's bèlè features bèlè dous and gran bèlè; Saint Lucia's bèlè includes bélè anlè and bélè matjé; Trinidad has over 14 types including Grand bélé and Congo bélé.
Bele descends from West African fertility dances, blended with European court dance elements and Caribbean cultural influences from the plantation era.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Bele is child of biguine: Bélé is the origin of biguine, a popular Martiniquan music and dance style.
Bele is child of chouval bwa: Chouval bwa evolved from bélé rhythms and instrumentation.
Bele is influence of zouk: Bélé influenced the development of zouk music and dance.
Bele is shares music of kompa: Kompa shares Caribbean rhythmic elements with bélé.
